blocks.text: The Tool Permissions lesson looked at a single moment, one tool call, one decision about whether to run it. Human in the loop workflows zoom out one level, to a whole multi step agentic workflow that might run for minutes or hours.
Instead of asking permission for every risky call along the way, the workflow runs on its own until it hits one specific point that truly needs a person, then it stops and waits.
This lesson covers how that pause works under the hood, how to design an approval screen a human can actually use quickly, and how to decide when a workflow needs a human at all.
1. From a Single Tool Call to a Whole Workflow

blocks.alt: An agent workflow runs autonomously until it reaches a sensitive step and pauses

blocks.text: Tool level permissions ask, should this one call run right now. Workflow level human in the loop asks a bigger question, should this entire multi step plan be allowed to reach its conclusion.

A workflow might call ten tools in a row without asking anyone anything, then hit an eleventh step that genuinely needs a human, refunding a customer, deleting a production record, sending an email to a whole mailing list.
Designing at the workflow level means picking that one moment deliberately, instead of interrupting the user at every single step along the way.
2. What Human in the Loop Actually Means
Human in the loop means a workflow is built so that, at a chosen point, control passes from the agent to a person, and the agent will not continue until that person responds.
It is not the same as just logging what the agent did after the fact. The workflow genuinely stops and waits, it does not proceed and hope someone notices later.

blocks.title: Not every check is human in the loop
blocks.content: A confirmation dialog that just restates what already happened is not a real checkpoint. Human in the loop only counts if the workflow cannot move forward until a person actually answers.

blocks.text: 3. Choosing Where to Pause

blocks.alt: A low risk step runs through while a high risk step pauses for review

blocks.text: Good pause points share a few traits, they are hard to undo, they touch money or people outside the system, or they are the last chance to catch a mistake before it becomes expensive.
A bad pattern is scattering pauses everywhere out of caution. That trains people to click approve without reading, which defeats the entire purpose.

items: Sending an email or message to someone outside the organization
Deleting or overwriting data that cannot be easily recovered
Spending money, issuing a refund, or placing an order
Changing a production configuration or deploying code
Taking any action that affects a person who never agreed to the workflow

blocks.text: 4. The Pending State: A Tool Call That Waits

blocks.alt: A tool call enters a pending state and waits for a human decision

blocks.text: A normal tool call returns a result the moment it finishes running. A human in the loop tool call is different, it returns immediately, but with a status that says it is still waiting, not that it succeeded or failed.
That pending status carries an identifier for the request, so the workflow, or a separate resume call later, can look it up and pick up exactly where it left off.

blocks.text: 5. What a Pending Response Looks Like in Code
Here is a tool that wants to issue a refund. Instead of issuing it right away, it creates an approval request and returns a pending state.
Nothing risky has happened yet. The only thing that ran was a record being created that says a human needs to look at this.
6. Resuming the Workflow Once a Human Decides

blocks.alt: A human decision resumes the paused workflow

blocks.text: A second function checks the decision and, only if it was approved, actually performs the refund and lets the workflow continue.
The workflow engine calls resume_after_decision either on a timer, or the moment a webhook tells it a human has responded.
7. Keeping State Alive While You Wait
A human might take thirty seconds or three days to respond, so the workflow cannot just hold everything in memory and hope the process stays running that whole time.
The safe pattern is to save the workflow state to durable storage the moment it pauses, then reload it when the decision comes back, rather than keeping the process itself alive and blocked.

blocks.title: Treat a pause like a checkpoint, not a sleep
blocks.content: Writing the paused state to a database or queue means a server restart, deploy, or crash while waiting does not lose the request. A workflow that just sleeps in memory will not survive any of those.

blocks.text: 8. Designing an Approval Interface People Can Trust
The approval screen is the entire point of this pattern, if it is confusing or buried in detail, people will approve things they have not actually understood.
A good approval interface answers four questions at a glance, without making the human dig for any of them.
9. What Goes on the Approval Screen

items: What action is being requested, in plain language, not a raw function name
Why the agent wants to take it, the reasoning or trigger that led here
What exactly will happen if approved, concrete numbers and names, not vague summaries
What happens if rejected, so the human knows nothing bad occurs by saying no

blocks.text: Showing the raw request payload alongside the plain language summary helps too, since it lets a careful reviewer double check the details match the story.
Keep the screen short enough to read in one glance. A wall of text defeats the goal of a fast, informed decision just as badly as missing information does.
10. Approve, Reject, and Edit Before Approving

blocks.alt: A human can approve, reject, or edit before approving a pending action

blocks.text: A binary approve or reject button covers most cases, but sometimes the request is almost right and only needs a small correction.
Letting a human edit the amount, the recipient, or the wording before approving avoids a wasteful reject and redo cycle, as long as the edited version is shown clearly before it runs.

blocks.text: 11. Timeouts, Reminders, and Silence
People get busy, requests get buried in a queue, and a workflow cannot wait forever without some kind of plan for silence.
A sensible design sets a timeout, sends one or two reminders before it expires, and defines clearly what happens if no one ever answers, usually treating it the same as a rejection.

blocks.title: Silence should never mean approval
blocks.content: If a workflow treats no response as a yes, it has quietly turned a human checkpoint back into full autonomy. Expired requests should default to the safer outcome, not the riskier one.

blocks.text: 12. Getting the Request in Front of the Right Human
An approval request that sits in a dashboard no one checks is not really a checkpoint, it just delays the workflow forever.
Route the request to wherever the right person already looks, a chat channel, an email, a mobile push notification, and route it to a specific role or on call person, not a shared inbox nobody owns.
If the first person cannot respond in time, escalate to a backup rather than letting the request expire by default.
13. When a Workflow Should Require a Human

blocks.alt: A workflow requiring a human is compared against one running fully autonomously

blocks.text: A human checkpoint earns its cost when the action is hard to reverse, affects someone outside the system, or when the agent itself is uncertain about the right move.

items: The action cannot be easily undone once it runs
Money changes hands, or a contract or legal commitment is created
A person outside the organization receives a message or a decision
The agent is operating outside the situations it was tested on
A mistake here would be expensive, embarrassing, or unsafe

blocks.text: 14. When a Workflow Should Run Fully Autonomously
Not every step deserves a human, and asking for approval on safe, reversible, low stakes actions just trains people to click through without reading.

items: The action is easy to reverse or has no lasting effect
The action only touches data inside a sandbox or test environment
The workflow has run the same pattern successfully many times before
The cost of a mistake is small compared to the cost of every delay

blocks.text: A good rule of thumb, if you would not bother mentioning the action to a colleague afterward, it probably does not need their approval beforehand either.
15. Building Risk Tiers Into the Workflow

blocks.alt: Low, medium, and high risk tiers each get a different level of human review

blocks.text: Instead of a single all or nothing rule, most production systems sort actions into a small number of risk tiers, each with its own behavior.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Tier","Example Actions","Human Required","Timeout Behavior"],"rows":[["Low","Reading data, drafting a message for later review","No","Not applicable"],["Medium","Sending an internal message, updating a non critical record","Optional, based on context","Auto approve after a short window"],["High","Refunds, deletions, external emails, deployments","Yes, always","Expire to rejected, notify again"]]}

blocks.text: This kind of tiering lets the same workflow engine serve both a quick internal tool and a high stakes production system, just by adjusting which tier each action falls into.
16. Audit Trails and Accountability
Every pause, decision, and resume should be recorded, who approved it, when, and what exact details they saw at the time.
This matters for more than compliance. When something goes wrong weeks later, the audit trail is what lets a team reconstruct exactly what was shown to the human and what they agreed to.

blocks.text: 17. Testing Human in the Loop Workflows
A pause point is easy to forget about in tests, since most test runs never have a real human sitting around to click approve.
Build a fake approver into your test suite, something that can auto approve, auto reject, or auto expire a request on command, so the resume path gets exercised on every run.

items: Test the pending response shape before anyone approves anything
Test resuming after an approval, and confirm the original action actually runs
Test resuming after a rejection, and confirm the action never runs
Test what happens when the timeout fires with no response at all

blocks.title: A workflow that only works in the happy path is not done
blocks.content: If your tests never exercise the rejected and expired branches, you will find out how they behave for the first time in production, on a request that actually mattered.

blocks.text: Worked Example
An agent handles customer support tickets. Most of its work, reading tickets, drafting replies, tagging categories, runs fully on its own.
When a ticket asks for a refund over fifty dollars, the agent calls issue_refund, gets back a pending status, and the workflow pauses right there.
A support lead sees a clear approval screen, the order, the amount, the customer message, and the agent reasoning, and approves it in under ten seconds.
The workflow resumes, runs process_refund, replies to the customer, and closes the ticket, all without the lead touching anything else in the process.
Common Mistakes

items: Asking for approval on every single step, which trains people to stop reading
Blocking a process in memory instead of saving state, losing the request on a restart
Showing a raw JSON payload with no plain language summary of what will happen
Treating a timeout or silence as approval instead of the safer rejection path
Routing requests to a shared inbox nobody actually monitors
Never recording who approved what, making later audits impossible

blocks.text: Practice
Take a workflow you already know, one with at least one risky step, and design a single human checkpoint for it.
Write out the pending response your tool would return, the fields on the approval screen, and what happens on a timeout, before writing any actual code.
Key Takeaway
Human in the loop workflows work by pausing at one deliberate point, returning a pending state instead of a result, and only continuing once a person makes a fast, well informed decision.
The skill is choosing that one point carefully, showing the human exactly what they need and nothing more, and treating fully autonomous steps as the default everywhere else.
